question: Is it obligatory to take medicine or undergo medical procedures?
asked: What is the ruling on availing ourselves of medicine and medical procedures? Is every single medicine or procedure obligatory, or can someone choose not to undertake a procedure? And if it is obligatory, to what extent must one go to do the procedure?
answer:
This is actually a very, very relevant and interesting question, and one that, frankly, one can give a very long talk about, but we don't have time. I'm going to summarize.

The Qur'an and the Sunnah obviously mention diseases and cures and medicines as well. Allah says in the Qur'an, on the tongue of Ibrahim (as): "When I fall sick, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala cures me." And Allah 'azza wa jall mentions a cure in the Qur'an, and that is of course honey, that Allah says:

> فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ

And our Prophet ﷺ said in a hadith in Musnad Imam Ahmad: "Allah has not sent down any disease except that He has also revealed with it a cure. Whoever knows it, knows it; whoever does not know it, does not know it." And in one version he added: "except for one, and that is death."

And this is actually very positive news for all researchers and all people that are working for cures: you have a guarantee that Allah 'azza wa jall has sent down a cure for every single disease, except for those people that are thinking they can cheat death. There is no cure for that.

And our Prophet ﷺ was asked by a Bedouin, "O Messenger of Allah, should we take medicine?" And he said, "Na'am, tadawaw ya 'ibad Allah. Yes, O servants of Allah, take medicine." This is a hadith in Abu Dawud. Literally he is saying, "Take medicine, for Allah has not revealed any disease except that He has revealed its cure."

One would extract from this, if one did not know usul al-fiqh, that taking medicine and medical procedures is wajib. And this is the common perception that most Muslims have: that if there is a medicine, I am obligated to take that medicine; if the doctors say I need to do surgery, I'm obliged to do surgery. However, this is a position that is simply not the position of any mainstream 'alim in the history of the ummah. Yes, one or two said it is wajib, but in reality none of the madhhabs and none of the famous 'ulama ever held this position.

The majority position is that taking medicine is either mubah, or, as the Shafi'is said, mustahab, or, the standard position of the Hanbalis, and Imam Ahmad was explicit: it is better to not take it. This is the position within the madhhabs. And this is not the time to go into all of the evidences and whatnot. I just want to clarify and emphasize: the claim that it is obligatory to take medicine and to follow medical procedures, that it is wajib and if you don't do it you are sinful, this is really a claim that is untenable in our Shari'ah. Rather, the standard position is that you may choose to take medicine and you may choose not to take medicine.

The Hanafis by and large seem to be somewhat ambivalent; sometimes they say it's mustahab. Ibn Hajar al-Haytami of the Shafi'is and al-Ramli both say that taking medicine is mustahab, but it is not wajib. Al-Dardir of the Maliki madhhab basically said it is permissible to take medicine, but then he does add that it might become obligatory in some circumstances, and we'll talk about that as well. And the standard position, as we said, of the Hanbalis (Ibn Muflih and Ibn Qudamah mentioned this): Imam Ahmad was explicit. He said, yes, it is permissible, but I prefer myself to not take it and to do tawakkul in Allah directly. This was his position.

Now, the Hanbalis have a number of evidences for this and whatnot. But the bottom line: to claim that it is wajib to take medicine is putting an unreasonable burden on the person, because hardly any medicine is guaranteed to be a cure. Almost every medicine has side effects, and, especially in America, medicine also has costs.

So the term wajib: we need to be less emotional and more academic. The term wajib means that if you do not do this, you will go to, maybe, Jahannam for not taking a procedure. And our scholars understand that these hadith about taking medicine indicate permissibility, or at most they indicate it's mustahab. To derive from this that it is wajib is not the position of any standard madhhab.

Now, when did some 'ulama say that it is wajib? They said: only if there is pretty much a certainty that taking the medication or doing the procedure will save you, and it is reasonable to do. It's not going to cost an arm and a leg; I don't mean financial cost, I mean emotional, the effort to come. If it is within your grasp, and there are fairly certain results that you shall be saved, out of a life-and-death scenario. And the example they give is: you have a wound that is gushing out, and all you need to do is to tie a tourniquet. In this case, even the Hanafis and the Shafi'is and some of the Malikis (the Malikis' position is official) say that you must, and if you don't, you might be sinful in that case. When the outcome is pretty certain, a matter of life and death, and the accessibility is right there, then it is almost a type of suicide to not take medicine. And that's why they said you must.

Otherwise, for the bulk of procedures and medication, is there a guarantee? Yes or no? No. It's uncertainty; it's percentage-based. And therefore, because of this, our scholars did not go down the route of saying taking medication is wajib. No, medicine does not prevent death in and of itself. It's a preponderance of evidence that generally it does so.

So the general rule therefore (and this is Ibn Taymiyyah's position as well) is that the default is that medicine and procedures are mustahab; you should do it. But there are times where it might even be makruh, and there are times where it might become wajib. This is Ibn Taymiyyah's position, and it seems to be the one that takes all of the evidences into it.

And of the evidences: why would the Qur'an tell us that honey is a cure? Why would the Prophet ﷺ tell us that hijama is a cure? Why would he tell us that the black seed is a cure, unless he wanted us to do it? So this is not just ja'iz; this is istihbab. It's mustahab.

Also, he himself ﷺ... By the way, it is not reported that he ever took any herbal medication, as far as we know, even though there might be a report from 'A'ishah from which we might be able to derive this. What we know for sure is that he did hijama on himself, and hijama is a medication. Also, there are numerous narrations from the Sahabah and Tabi'un that they would take medication and do medical procedures.

And there is the theological point that we believe, generally speaking, living longer with iman is better than living shorter with the same amount of iman, right? The hadith says, "ma yazidu al-mu'min": the mu'min only increases in goodness with his life, whatever is happening. A longer life will give you time to do more good deeds. So the general rule is that if you're able to, you should.

And it might be wajib if the procedure is within your grasp, and there are no impeding factors for you to not do it, and not doing it is pretty much a certainty of death. In this case, some 'ulama would say that it is wajib.

However, if there are factors that prevent this from being wajib, it might even be makruh. For example, a simple example: the side effects might be so painful and bad that it's not a marked difference from what you are upon. May Allah protect us all, but cancer, a severe type of cancer, and a person says, "I don't want to go through all of this with a 50-50 chance." Are we going to say it's wajib for him, that he has to undergo it? It's a 50-50 chance, and you know what the side effects are. You know you have to take medication for the side effects of the medication for the side effects of the medication; multiple layers of side effects are going to take place because of radiation. And some people are like, "I don't want to do it."

And my own teacher, Ibn 'Uthaymin, when he fell sick with cancer, the year after I studied with him, he came to America for treatment. The king sent him; it was the only time he visited America. He went to Boston, and he asked the doctors about the percentage and about the side effects, and he said, "I don't want the treatment." He had stomach cancer. He said, "I don't want the treatment. This is going to cause this side effect; I'm going to lose all of my hair; it's going to cause me to vomit, this and that. I've lived a good life." And so he went back without doing the treatment, and he passed away within two months. He had the option.

You cannot say it's wajib, because when you say wajib, you are saying that you have to do it. What if somebody living in this country, the bill is going to be $200,000, and the guy has $200,000 in his 401k, and he's like, "I need this money for my kids. I've lived a good life, alhamdulillah." If you say it's wajib, think about the implications. If you say it's wajib, you're going to say he has to spend all of his money (I'm just giving an example) for a procedure that might be 50-50, 70-30, at the expense of the lifelong savings he has for his children. No, it's not wajib. He is not throwing himself into suicide. He might put his trust in Allah, drink Zamzam, make du'a. It's not wajib to undertake medicine.

Also, and this is a very key factor we as Muslims need to look at, which by and large this culture does not look at: and that is the quality of life. This culture and these medical practices are obsessed with elongating life regardless of the cost. And we accept that death is going to happen. And we have to ask ourselves: at some point, a sick patient, the quality of life is so sad that it's just best to let them go with dignity. And this is especially the case if they have feeding tubes, if they have this, if they have that, and they're conscious.

We're not talking about the unconscious and pulling the plug. That is a question I will answer; the fiqh council just gave a fatwa about this, and that's a separate scenario. We're not asking that. Now we're talking about a conscious person, and he has a whole list of medication and tubes and whatnot, and he's like, "You know what, I'm sick of this. Just get me off of this. Let me just live my life with dignity." Is he sinful? No, he is not. Because at some point you weigh the quality of life against elongating it. At that quality, of what use is it?

This society is obsessed with life at the cost of the quality of life. They don't care, which is why it's so difficult for many of them to understand. For us, no: what is the purpose of living a few months longer if life is so painful and miserable? It's not wajib.

And therefore the bottom line is that if a person chooses to not do medical procedures that are, percentage-wise, 70, 90, even 90-10, it's not wajib. Maybe it would only be wajib if death is inevitable and it is reasonable to do the opposite. As I said, the simple example that is given: the blood is gushing out, all you've got to do is tie the tourniquet or do something that's going to stop it, and you intentionally just let it go out after a wound. Then you are really acting foolishly. Otherwise, other than this, **the general default is that it is mustahab, but it is not wajib to do medical procedures.**
